questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a two-case comparison controlled
questions.learningObjective: identify the feature that separates a controlled comparison from a pairing
questions.stem: Two districts recorded near-identical rainfall through one growing season, and a report asks why stream flow fell further in one of them. What has to be true for this to be a controlled comparison rather than a pairing?

options.text: The two are alike on the conditions the explanation depends on, and differ on the feature whose effect is being examined
The two differ in every other respect, so that nothing besides the feature of interest could produce the difference in flow
options.misconception: believes a controlled comparison needs the cases to be identical everywhere else, which would leave nothing left to compare

options.text: The two are described in the same words and measured with the same instrument, so that the record of each is equally detailed
options.misconception: treats consistent measurement and vocabulary as what makes a comparison controlled rather than the relation between the cases

options.text: The two were observed by the same team in the same weeks, so that each account rests on equally fresh records of what happened
options.misconception: confuses equal evidence-gathering effort with a design that holds conditions constant

questions.explanation: A controlled comparison is one in which the cases are matched on whatever the explanation depends on, and vary on the feature whose effect is being tested, so that a difference in the outcome cannot be read off the matching instead. The first option says exactly that. The second demands total difference everywhere else, which is the opposite requirement and would make any shared factor a rival explanation. The third confuses the quality of the record with the relation between the cases: two well-measured cases can still differ on every relevant condition, and two badly described ones can still be matched. The fourth treats equal effort as a design property, when effort affects how much each case can be trusted but not whether a rival condition is under control.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to differ between the cases for the outcome difference to be informative.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Distinguishing a controlled pair from a juxtaposition
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a controlled comparison from accounts merely set beside each other
questions.stem: A report sets two accounts of similar events side by side under a shared heading. What is missing before those two accounts count as a comparison?

options.text: A reason the cases are comparable, worked out before the accounts were chosen, so that the two are cases of the same thing
An equal length for each account, so that the reader gets a fair chance to weigh the two
options.misconception: takes equal space as what makes a comparison fair, when fairness is a property of the cases and not of the page

options.text: A shared country or region, so that the two settings are removed as rival explanations
options.misconception: believes a common setting substitutes for a worked-out basis of comparability, which is the work itself

options.text: A shared reader, so that one pair of eyes applies the same standard to both accounts
options.misconception: treats the identity of the audience as the thing that turns a pairing into an analysis

questions.explanation: Two accounts placed next to each other become a comparison only when the analyst can say why they are cases of the same thing, and can say it from conditions recorded independently of the outcomes rather than from the outcome itself. The first option names that requirement, including the ordering, since comparability established after reading the accounts can be anything the analyst finds convenient. The second is about presentation: a longer account may be better documented and says nothing about whether the cases match. The third mistakes a shared setting for a controlled one, when a common location is precisely where unnoticed differences in who is affected are easiest to miss. The fourth makes the audience the mechanism, and the standard a reader applies can be identical for two cases that share nothing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two were matched on something recorded before anyone saw the result.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A variable measured the same way in two cases
questions.learningObjective: choose measurement that makes a variable the same variable in both cases
questions.stem: A team wants one variable tracked across two ports, so that the two figures can be set beside each other. Which measurement choice delivers that?

options.text: The share of arriving vessels held at the quay more than an hour, defined once and counted from the same fields in both ports
The share of arriving vessels held at the quay, with each port's own threshold for holding left as that port records it
options.misconception: assumes a shared label makes the figures comparable while each port's threshold actually sets the standard

options.text: The number of vessels arriving, since a count of vessels is the one figure both ports already record alike
options.misconception: picks a figure that is easy to count and cannot carry the question the comparison is about

options.text: The share of arrivals held, defined once but counted only in the port whose log happens to be complete
options.misconception: defines the measure carefully and then measures it in one case only

questions.explanation: Two figures are the same measure only when the rule that produced them is the same rule, which means a single definition applied to comparable records in both cases. The first option does that and says so twice, once in the definition and once in where the count comes from. The second keeps the label and drops the rule, so a port that calls forty minutes a hold and one that calls ninety a hold produce figures that look like the same measure and are not. The third chooses the count that is easiest to get and least relevant, which is a common way for a comparison to end up measuring volume rather than performance. The fourth is careful about definition and careless about coverage, and a figure from one case is not a comparison even when it is the right figure.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule that produced each number would be written the same way twice.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contextual difference behind a diverging outcome
questions.learningObjective: attribute a diverging outcome to a documented difference in context
questions.stem: A booking system that removed a paper step cut waiting times in one region and left them unchanged in another, where the paper step had been paying for a clerk whose job was to complete each booking. What best explains the difference?

options.text: In the second region the removed step was the last thing that finished a booking, so removing it removed a task rather than a delay
The two regions measured waiting differently, so the flat figure in the second region is an artefact of its own counting practice
options.misconception: seeks the difference in the instruments rather than in what the two regions were actually doing

options.text: The second region has more clinics per clerk, so the same reduction in paperwork had further to travel before it reached a booking
options.misconception: invents a staffing ratio the passage does not mention and leaves the described clerk unexplained

options.text: The first region introduced the system earlier, so its waiting times had longer to fall before anyone looked again
options.misconception: supplies a timing difference the passage never reports in order to avoid the explanation it does supply

questions.explanation: An intervention that removes a step produces an improvement only if the step was what was producing the delay, and the passage states that in the second region the paper step was paying for the person who finished the booking. Removing it there removes the completion task itself, so waiting time stays where it was. The first option names that mechanism and ties it to the documented detail. The second looks for the difference in measurement, which would leave the passage's account of the clerk unexplained and treats the null result as a reporting problem. The third reaches for a ratio the passage never gives, which is a common way of avoiding a detail the passage has already handed over. The fourth introduces a date the passage does not mention, and a date difference would not explain a flat outcome anyway.
questions.hint: Find the detail in the passage that says what the removed step was doing in each region.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Claiming a mechanism and testing it elsewhere
questions.learningObjective: define a mechanism, then say how a second case could test the one claimed
questions.stem: A first study argues that a change in the way shifts were handed over produced fewer missed handovers. First say what a mechanism is, then say what a second case would have to show to test the one claimed.

options.text: The step-by-step route from the change to the outcome, and that the second case shows each step occurring in the order the route requires
A measurable association between the change and the outcome, and that the second case reproduces the association at a larger size
options.misconception: substitutes a bigger association for the route the first study claimed between change and outcome

options.text: The change itself as it was introduced, and that the second case repeats that same change under the same conditions
options.misconception: makes the test a repetition of the treatment and leaves the claimed route untested

options.text: The population the first study sampled, and that the second case draws its sample from that same population
options.misconception: treats matching the sample as the test, which is a check on the first study and not on the mechanism

questions.explanation: A mechanism is the ordered chain of steps that carries a change to an outcome, and a second case tests it by showing whether each of those steps is present in the expected order there. The first option defines the mechanism as a route and specifies the evidence that would confirm the route. The second offers an association at larger size, which is what a mechanism claim is usually offered in place of, since a bigger association says nothing about the steps. The third proposes repeating the intervention, which estimates an effect rather than tracing a route. The fourth proposes matching the sample, which is a useful check on the original study and does not touch the chain the study asserted.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be visible at each stage for the claimed route to be credible.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: When a finding may be carried to another context
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a finding from one setting may be applied in another
questions.stem: A study of one region's grant scheme is cited as settling how grant schemes work in general. What does that use of the study overlook?

options.text: The study supports a claim about a scheme in one particular place, which carries elsewhere only where the conditions that produced it are also met
The study's sample was small, which can be settled by running the same study again with more participants
options.misconception: makes sample size the only obstacle and leaves the question of whether the setting was part of the result

options.text: Other regions might simply prefer different schemes, which makes the question one of local taste rather than of transfer
options.misconception: turns a question about conditions into a question about preference and so removes it from empirical dispute

options.text: The study is now several years old, so only work published more recently can settle a general claim
options.misconception: treats recency as the test of whether a finding still applies, which is not what age of a study changes

questions.explanation: A finding is a claim about the world that was produced in a particular setting, and it travels as far as the conditions that produced it travel. The first option says that, and it also says the right thing about a study cited for a general claim: the study can be sound and still not license the general version. The second names a real limitation but picks the one that a repeat run could address, and a repeat in the same setting leaves the transfer question untouched. The third makes the transfer question unanswerable by relocating it to taste, which is a move that protects a general claim from being tested. The fourth confuses the age of a study with the range of its claim, neither of which is fixed by publication date.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true of the new setting for the study's result to be expected there.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: One concept, two words, two sets of cases
questions.learningObjective: check whether two terms in different languages of theory select the same cases
questions.stem: A term from one theoretical language is rendered in another with a word that also names a specific practice in the receiving discipline. What has to be settled before the two are used as the same concept?

options.text: Whether the two terms pick out the same instances, since two words can name one thing in one field and a narrower practice in another
Whether the two terms sound similar in both languages, since the sound carries the technical meaning across
options.misconception: believes phonetic similarity is what a shared technical sense depends on

options.text: Whether the two terms were both written down before either discipline existed as a separate field
options.misconception: makes the age of a term a condition on its having a stable referent

options.text: Whether the two terms can be made to appear in one sentence together, since context alone fixes what a word means
options.misconception: assumes juxtaposition in a sentence settles a question that each field's own usage decides

questions.explanation: A concept is a rule for which cases count, and two words used as though they were one concept will agree on a claim only if they admit the same instances. The first option states that test. The second confuses a linguistic resemblance with a shared referent, and the sound of a technical term is a poor guide to which cases it covers. The third makes the history of a term decisive when usage is what settles the referent, and both fields change what their words cover over time. The fourth treats a shared sentence as resolving the matter, when the sentence is written by whoever is doing the translating and so carries that writer's usage into both sides.
questions.hint: Ask whether one instance a practitioner would call the second term would also be called by the first.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two fields counting at different levels
questions.learningObjective: identify a mismatch of unit of analysis between two accounts of the same subject
questions.stem: One member of a seminar counts how many of a city's bus routes arrive within the published timetable, and another counts how many passengers report missing a connection on the routes they used. The two figures are then presented side by side as a single picture of the network. What is the actual difficulty?

options.text: The two counts sit at different levels, so a route is what one number describes and a passenger is what the other describes, and the pair answers two questions
The two drew on different records, so the disagreement will disappear once both counts are taken from the same source
options.misconception: believes a shared source would make a route count and a passenger count interchangeable

options.text: The two measured in different weeks, so a shared date would put the two figures on the same footing
options.misconception: dates the difference without support from the passage and leaves the level mismatch in place

options.text: The two used different words for punctuality, so only the wording of the two measures is in dispute
options.misconception: reduces a difference in what is being counted to a difference in how it is labelled

questions.explanation: Putting two figures together requires that they describe the same thing at the same level, and here the first counts routes and the second counts people, so the two numbers are answering different questions about the same network and neither is a check on the other. The first option names the mismatch precisely. The second treats a shared data source as a cure, when the cure would be to count the same object twice. The third supplies a timing difference the passage does not mention, and a common week would still leave a route being weighed against a passenger. The fourth makes the issue one of vocabulary, and it is not: a passenger missing a connection and a route arriving late are different events, whatever either is called.
questions.hint: Ask what single object each of the two numbers is counting.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing a typical case and choosing a deviant one
questions.learningObjective: say what a typical case is for, then what a deviant case is for
questions.stem: A group can study only one case in depth. First say what a case selected because it is typical is for, then say what a case selected because it is deviant is for.

options.text: Describing how a pattern holds in the ordinary run of cases, and pinning down what an explanation must account for in the case that breaks it
Putting the explanation to the hardest available test, and summarising the ordinary run of cases for background
options.misconception: swaps the purposes, so a typical case is asked to do a test it cannot do and a deviant one is used as background

options.text: Covering as many further cases as possible, and saving the group time by leaving awkward material unstudied
options.misconception: treats a single case as a way of covering many and mistakes convenience for methodological purpose

options.text: Avoiding the charge of choosing a case to suit the explanation, and replacing that check with a second case of the same kind
options.misconception: takes one case as a guard against cherry-picking and never applies the guard to a case chosen for its results

questions.explanation: A typical case carries the ordinary run of cases, so it is the right choice when the question is how a pattern actually looks in practice, and a deviant case is the right choice when the question is what an explanation has to survive, because a case where the expected result fails to appear forces the explanation to say what else is going on. The first option gives each case its proper job. The second swaps them, and a deviant case summarised as background is the one case that should not be summarised. The third treats case work as coverage, which is what a sample gives and not what a case does. The fourth claims one case guards against selection, and a case picked for its results is exactly the situation a second look is meant to catch.
questions.hint: Ask which case you would choose if the question were about the ordinary run, and which if it were about the limits of the explanation.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Matching cases as closely as possible
questions.learningObjective: say what a matched comparison gains and what it cannot settle
questions.stem: A design chooses cases that are as alike as it can make them, and varies only the feature under study. What does that buy the analysis, and what does it leave open?

options.text: It makes an observed difference harder to explain away, and it leaves the finding's reach beyond those cases unsettled
It makes an observed difference easier to explain away, and it settles how far the finding reaches beyond the cases chosen
options.misconception: reverses both halves, treating a tight match as both weaker evidence and wider scope

options.text: It widens the range of settings a finding covers, and it makes the observed difference harder to read
options.misconception: credits a narrow match with breadth, which is the one thing a tight match cannot give

options.text: It settles whether a mechanism operates, and it leaves the reach of the finding open
options.misconception: claims a tight match traces the mechanism, which needs ordered evidence about steps rather than matched cases

questions.explanation: Matching cases tightly means that whatever else might produce the outcome is reduced in both, so a difference that still appears is harder to attribute to anything else, and the price is that the evidence speaks with confidence about the cases it covers and says less about others. The first option states the trade in both directions. The second reverses it, and a match that leaves fewer rival explanations certainly does not widen the claim. The third credits the design with breadth it cannot deliver, since narrow cases are the reason breadth is missing. The fourth attributes a mechanism test to case design, and mechanisms are traced through ordered evidence about steps, which a matched pair does not supply.
questions.hint: Ask what the tight match has removed, and what it therefore cannot tell you.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Choosing cases that differ on nearly everything
questions.learningObjective: say what a most-different comparison gains and what it cannot settle
questions.stem: A design chooses cases that differ on nearly every feature except the one under study. What does that buy the analysis, and what does it leave open?

options.text: It makes an observed similarity harder to explain away, and it leaves open whether the feature alone produced it
It makes an observed similarity easier to explain away, and it settles that the feature alone produced it
options.misconception: reverses both halves and credits a wide contrast with the attribution it cannot deliver

options.text: It reduces the number of routes to the outcome, and it settles the mechanism without further evidence
options.misconception: treats a hard-to-match pair as a shorter causal chain, which is what case selection cannot do

options.text: It makes the two cases representative of their settings, and it removes the need to hold anything constant
options.misconception: credits contrast cases with representativeness and treats contrast as if it were control

questions.explanation: Cases chosen to differ on everything else put a heavy burden on any explanation of a similarity, because so many conditions change at once that a shared result is unlikely to be a coincidence, and they also make attribution hard, since the cases differ in many things that might matter. The first option gives the gain and the cost. The second reverses both. The third treats a difficult pair as a short chain of steps, and mechanisms are established by evidence about the order steps occurred, not by the number of things that differ. The fourth confuses two designs that answer different questions, and choosing cases to be unlike each other says nothing about how well either represents its own setting.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the similarity surprising, and what that same feature does to the explanation.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chosen case pair can be claimed to show
questions.learningObjective: identify what a case pair is, then state the strongest inference it licenses
questions.stem: Two cases have been chosen, and a researcher is about to state what the pair supports. First say what makes this a case pair, then say the strongest inference the pair licenses.

options.text: Cases selected on features recorded before the evidence was seen, and a claim that the feature shaped the outcome in each of the two
Cases selected because their results were informative, and a claim that the feature shaped the outcome across the population
options.misconception: selects on the outcome and then claims a population result, which is both a selection problem and a scope problem

options.text: Cases taken from the largest settings available, and a claim that the size of the setting produced the outcome
options.misconception: substitutes availability for selection logic and then attributes the result to the setting's size

options.text: Cases with the most complete records, and a claim that the feature would work the same way in a third case
options.misconception: chooses on data quality and then claims a case nobody has studied yet

The first option states both halves and keeps the claim at the level the selection supports. The second selects on the outcome, which is where a researcher's own expectations enter without notice, and then makes a population claim on top. The third picks what was available rather than what would test the explanation. The fourth chooses cases that document well and then extends to an unstudied third, which no pair can do.
questions.hint: Ask what was known about each case before anyone knew its result.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence behind each step of a traced sequence
questions.learningObjective: assess a process-tracing claim step by step against the evidence offered for each step
questions.stem: A study of a metering programme claims three steps: officials decided to meter, the decision reached field staff, and field staff acted on it. Its evidence is a minute recording the decision, two recollections that the message reached them, gathered a year later, and a rise in notices issued after the decision. What is the state of this tracing?

options.text: The first step rests on a record made at the time, the second on accounts produced long afterwards, and the third on a change that other causes could also produce
All three steps are equally supported, since a minute, a recollection, and a change in notices are each evidence of a step
options.misconception: levels three kinds of evidence as equal and so lets a route stand on its weakest link

options.text: The first step is the weakest, because a minute records what officials decided rather than what they did
options.misconception: inverts the ordering, treating a contemporaneous record as weaker than a later account of a different link

options.text: The second step is the strongest, since two people agreeing about the same message is harder to get wrong than one document
options.misconception: prefers agreement between recollections to a contemporaneous record and overlooks when they were produced

questions.explanation: A traced sequence is only as strong as its weakest link, and the three pieces of evidence here differ sharply in what they can support. The first option says what each one is: a minute made at the time records the decision itself, recollections gathered a year afterwards are a reconstruction with no check on it, and a rise in notices is an outcome that would follow from other causes. The second treats the three as interchangeable, which is how a chain gets asserted without support. The third inverts the ranking by judging a decision on whether it became an action, which is a question about a different step. The fourth prefers two agreeing recollections to a contemporaneous record, and agreement between two people asked a year later can be produced by the same misremembering or the same earlier telling.

options.text: The claim survives provided the missing link is named as unobserved, since disclosing a gap is enough to keep the sequence intact

options.text: The two observed steps should be dropped as well, since evidence for a later step is worthless once an earlier one is unproven

questions.topic: Several routes to the same visible outcome
questions.learningObjective: name the pattern of several routes reaching one outcome, then say how a study should proceed
questions.stem: Several organisations reached the same visible outcome by different routes. First say what that pattern is, then say what a study of it should do.

Confounding, and add a third organisation that differs in its outcome rather than in its route
options.misconception: names a pattern of shared cause and answers it by looking at a different end of the process

options.text: Selection, and restrict the study to the organisations that reached the outcome soonest
options.misconception: names a problem of who entered the study and answers it by choosing on the outcome

options.text: Agreement, and check that the routes reach the outcome in the same order of steps
options.misconception: treats several routes to one outcome as mutual support, when only one shared step would support that

The third discards the record for the interest that also explains why it exists, which would empty most of the archive. The fourth rules it out entirely, and an unusable step is not the same as a missing one.
questions.hint: Ask which feature of the document supports it and which feature limits it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Opposite results across two cases
questions.learningObjective: respond to a cross-case contradiction without discarding the offending case
questions.stem: Two cases show opposite relationships between a practice and an outcome: in one the practice accompanies a better result, in the other a worse one. Which response is sound?

options.text: Treat the disagreement as a finding about the settings and ask what differs between them that could reverse the relationship
Publish both results and let readers weigh them, since two cases cannot resolve a disagreement between themselves
options.misconception: suspends interpretation and hands the reader a contradiction with nothing to hold on to

options.text: Publish the case with the larger effect, since the better-studied case is the one worth relying on
options.misconception: chooses on effect size and presents a selection as a conclusion

options.text: Publish only the case that fits the expected pattern, since a pattern needs cases that agree
options.misconception: removes the counterexample and reports the remainder as a pattern

questions.explanation: A relationship that reverses between two cases is not a nuisance to be managed, it is information: it says that whatever the two cases share is not doing the work, and the productive question is which difference between them could matter. The first option takes it that way. The second leaves the reader holding a contradiction, and a study's job includes saying what the contradiction would have to mean. The third chooses a case on effect size, and a larger effect is not a better-studied case. The fourth discards the case that disagrees, and a pattern built by discarding is the one the other case was chosen to test.
questions.hint: Ask what the two cases share, given that the relationship reversed between them.

questions.topic: One word carrying two established senses
questions.learningObjective: state the cost of a term used in two senses within the same analysis
questions.stem: Two disciplines use the same word, in one for a formal arrangement and in the other for any practice that follows a habit. What is the cost of using the word in both senses in a single analysis?

options.text: A claim can pass from what follows a habit to what is formally arranged, with nothing in the text marking the change of sense
The word loses its ordinary meaning, so readers outside both disciplines lose the term altogether
options.misconception: predicts damage to non-specialist readers from an ambiguity that specialists can and do handle

options.text: The two disciplines are shown to agree, since a shared word is evidence of a shared phenomenon
options.misconception: reads a shared label as shared substance

options.text: Nothing, provided the word is defined once at the start of the analysis
options.misconception: believes one definition can cover two established senses at once

questions.explanation: Using one word for a formal arrangement and for any habitual practice lets a claim about habit do the work of a claim about arrangement, or the reverse, and nothing in the writing records the slide. The first option names that. The second predicts a loss for outside readers, which is a real cost of jargon but not the one at issue, since specialists would still slide between the senses. The third treats a shared word as evidence, and the two disciplines may be describing the same word's history rather than the same thing. The fourth offers a single definition as a remedy, and a definition cannot cover two senses that other work in the same field uses differently.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The strongest claim a matched pair supports
questions.learningObjective: state the limit of an inference drawn from a matched pair
questions.stem: A matched pair differs on the practice and not on any recorded background feature, and the outcome differs as well. What is the strongest claim the pair supports?

options.text: That the outcome differed in these two cases along with the practice, with the recorded background held still and the unrecorded factors left open
That the practice causes the outcome in general, since the pair has removed every other explanation
options.misconception: claims to have removed the unrecorded factors, which matching on recorded features cannot do

options.text: That the practice causes the outcome wherever the background is similar, since that is what matching establishes
options.misconception: extends a two-case result to a whole class of settings on the strength of a matched pair

options.text: That the practice had no effect, since two cases differing in unrecorded ways cannot show anything
options.misconception: turns unrecorded differences into a demonstration of no effect

questions.explanation: A matched pair fixes the features that were recorded and measured, and the features that were neither recorded nor measured remain available as alternative explanations, so the pair supports a claim about the two cases with its limits stated. The first option states that claim with the limit inside it. The second claims the elimination of everything, which is not what matching does. The third extends to a class of settings, and no pair of cases licenses a claim about every setting that shares their background. The fourth inverts the residual problem into a finding of no effect, and unrecorded differences weaken a causal claim without establishing its opposite.
questions.hint: Ask which differences between the two cases were never measured.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A coincident change offered as a cause
questions.learningObjective: identify the causal claim defeated by a second change in the same period
questions.stem: A report states that after a clinic added evening hours, more patients were seen within a week of referral, that the increase began the same week the hours were added, and that because the hours were added deliberately, the extended hours are taken to be the cause. In the same weeks the referral service began sending reminder texts. What is wrong with the causal claim?

The increase began the same week rather than a week later, and a cause ought to show its effect after some delay
options.misconception: sets a requirement for delay that causes are not obliged to meet

options.text: The clinic was not observed before the hours were added, so the report has no baseline against which the increase can be judged
options.misconception: raises a missing before-measurement that the report's own statement of an increase does not suggest

options.text: The claim is sound, because a change adopted on purpose is a change that counts as a cause
options.misconception: treats the intention behind a change as the thing that identifies it as a cause

The first option names the rival the report had before it and the reason timing cannot separate them. The second invents a delay requirement, and a cause can act within the week it appears. The third objects to a missing baseline that the report's own account of an increase implies it had. The fourth mistakes a reason for adopting a change for a reason it produced the result.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why the conditions belong inside a finding
questions.learningObjective: justify treating a finding's conditions as part of the claim itself
questions.stem: Explain why a finding's conditions are part of the finding rather than an accompanying note about how it was obtained.

answer.exemplar: A finding states that under these conditions this happened, and the conditions are not decoration on that statement but the terms that make it true, in the way that a claim about one material holds only of that material. Strip them out and what remains is not a shorter version of the finding but a different and much larger claim, because a result with no conditions attached is a claim about everywhere, and a claim about everywhere is refuted by the first setting that fails without anyone having made a mistake. This is why the conditions belong inside the claim: they are what tells a reader where to stop. A reader who is deciding whether the finding applies to their own setting needs exactly that, and a conditions section consulted separately is in the wrong place for it, because the reader meets the claim in the results and rarely travels to the methods to discover what it is bounded by. Putting the conditions in the claim also protects the analyst. A research report that states the conditions in the claim has made its own reach visible, which means anyone extending it has to say what they are adding and why they think the conditions still hold. A report that keeps them in the methods has instead left the extension to whoever quotes the sentence, and the sentence will travel alone. The costs run the other way too. A claim with conditions attached can accumulate: another condition that holds extends it, and two findings with different conditions can be brought together once the reader can see both. This is also what makes a rival case informative. When a study reports a case that met the conditions and produced nothing, the reader knows the result is about the mechanism rather than about the conditions, and a report that never stated the conditions leaves the reader unable to tell which of the two has been weakened.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that conditions set where a claim stops, that removing them converts a bounded finding into a universal claim that the first counterexample refutes, and that keeping them in the claim is what lets a reader check whether the finding reaches their own case.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would be entitled to claim if the conditions were left out.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a comparison cannot be made to say
questions.learningObjective: justify a limit on the inferences a case comparison licenses
questions.stem: Explain why a comparison of two carefully matched cases cannot by itself establish that the same relationship holds in general.

answer.exemplar: A comparison establishes what happened in the cases it examined, and the care taken in matching them makes that result hard to dismiss without looking for a case, but care in matching buys strength about the cases and not reach beyond them. The reason is that matching works on the features that were recorded. Anything the analyst did not write down was neither held still nor deliberately varied, so it remains free to differ between the two cases and to differ in a third case as well, which means a comparison can be a strong finding and a narrow claim at the same time. To reach a general claim, something else is needed, and the usual candidates are each limited in their own way. Adding cases increases the number of instances on which the relationship was seen and says nothing about the instances not examined, so a pattern observed in a dozen places is still a statement about those places. Finding a case where the relationship fails shows the reach stops somewhere, and a reader who knows the boundary respects it more than one who does not. Averaging across cases hides the boundary rather than locating it. This is also why the number of cases in a comparison is not a measure of how general its result is: two matched cases and twelve matched cases differ in how much work has been done, and a third case that behaves like the first two adds less to the claim than a single case that does not, which is why a case chosen for disagreement is often worth more than a case chosen for agreement. What a comparison licenses is a claim about cases, and the argument from those cases to other cases is a separate step, to be made explicitly and with a reason for why it is safe to make.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that matching holds fixed only the features that were recorded, that unrecorded differences remain available as rival explanations, and that extending the claim to other cases is a further argument rather than a property of the matched pair.
questions.hint: Ask which differences between the two cases were never written down.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Fixing the unit of analysis before choosing cases
questions.learningObjective: identify what must be fixed about a comparison before any case is chosen
questions.stem: Two colleagues propose to compare how fairly a service is treated. Before any case is chosen, what has to be fixed?

options.text: What the unit of comparison is, such as a person, an appointment, or a household, since the same records favour different readings at each level
How many cases to choose, since the number of cases sets how far a disagreement can be checked
options.misconception: settles the size of the evidence before settling what the evidence is about

options.text: Which fields to record, since the fields decide what can be compared at all
options.misconception: settles the record's contents without settling what each counted record stands for

options.text: What counts as fair, since the evaluative standard has to be settled before anything is measured
options.misconception: settles the standard of judgement and leaves the object being counted open

questions.explanation: A count of people and a count of appointments from the same records can support opposite readings of whether a service is fair, and the choice of unit is what decides which, so it has to be settled before cases are chosen rather than noticed once the figures are in. The first option says that. The second settles the amount of evidence before its subject. The third settles the fields without saying what a record in those fields represents, and the same fields support different readings at different levels. The fourth fixes the evaluative standard, which is necessary and not sufficient, since a standard applied to an unset unit is applied to nothing in particular.
questions.hint: Ask what one counted record stands for in each of the two readings.
